idiom_name: def initialize(repo: SqlOrderRepository.new, clock: Clock.new) + boot-time wiring
implementation_notes: The Ruby realization is a plain initializer with keyword arguments defaulted to the production collaborator, so callers can always pass a double and no container is involved. What replaces the injector is the handful of lines that construct the object graph in a boot file or framework initializer; dry-auto_inject/dry-container provide the gem-based variant where a class includes Import['repo'] and .new resolves from the container. Constructor injection is the norm; setters serve genuinely optional collaborators.
pitfalls: Default arguments construct the real collaborator - a heavy default (DB connection, HTTP client) runs in tests that forget to override it.
Class-level memoisation (||=) hides global state that survives across examples and defeats substitution.
Referencing concrete constants inside the class body hard-wires them; inject the object instead of resolving it lazily.

variants.name: dry-auto_inject with a Dry::Core::Container
variants.idiom_name: Dry::AutoInject(container) Import with container-resolved constructor dependencies
variants.implementation_notes: dry-auto_inject generates .new/#initialize per class so constructor dependencies are resolved from a container by name, while keyword arguments still override any dependency for tests; Dry::Core::Container is the thread-safe registry holding the objects. What replaces hand-written wiring is the include Import['repos.orders'] declaration plus the registrations, centralising composition and supporting dry-system component hierarchies. Choose it when several entry points and environments must swap registrations systematically; keyword defaults alone are simpler.
variants.code_sketch:
Import = Dry::AutoInject(MyContainer)

class OrderService
  include Import['repositories.orders', 'clock']
  # .new resolves both from MyContainer; pass repo: to override
end

OrderService.new(clock: Clock.new).repo   # explicit override still works
pitfalls: Container keys are strings: a typo surfaces at resolution time (or boot) rather than at definition time.
Injected dependencies become instance readers, so naming clashes silently shadow behaviour.
